title: Which Filipino Farmer Community Should You Join for Advice and Farm Inputs?
metaTitle: Filipino Farmer Community: Where to Join and Buy Inputs
metaDescription: Which Filipino farmer community is worth joining? Compare coops, DA programs and online groups for advice and inputs, and what anee.io offers for free.
excerpt: The best Filipino farmer community is the one where real growers near you answer your questions, and where membership gets you cheaper inputs. For most farmers that means two memberships: a registered cooperative or association for inputs and DA programs, and an online group for daily advice. anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, has a free community inside the same app that runs your season, but it does not sell inputs.

blocks.text:
Farming alone is expensive. You pay retail for fertilizer, you guess at a new pest, and you learn about a good buyer after your harvest is gone. A community fixes part of that, but only if you pick the right one for the right job.

So split the question in two. Where do you get advice and contacts? And where do you get inputs at a better price? The answers are usually different groups.

items: Cheaper inputs come through cooperatives, farmers' associations and DA programs, not through social media groups.
RSBSA registration is free and makes you eligible for DA help such as seeds, fertilizer, loans and crop insurance.
An online Filipino farmer community is best for quick advice, early pest warnings and new contacts.
anee.io has no separate premium community fee. The community comes with every plan, including the free Libre plan.

blocks.text: What makes a good Filipino farmer community?
A big group is not always a good group. Before you join, or before you pay, check these points. They work for a barangay association, a Facebook group or an app.

blocks.text: Where can you buy farm inputs as a group?

If your goal is lower prices on seed, fertilizer and chemicals, an online group will not do much. Instead, the savings come from buying together and from government programs. These are the usual doors.

items.title: Register in the RSBSA
items.text: The Registry System for Basic Sectors in Agriculture is the DA list of farmers, farm workers and fisherfolk. Get the form from your city or municipal agriculture office. Registration is voluntary, free and a lifetime enrollment.

items.title: Join a cooperative or association
items.text: A cooperative registered with the Cooperative Development Authority can buy inputs in volume and borrow as a group. Ask about the membership fee or share capital before you join, and ask what members received last season.

items.title: Ask the agriculture office about programs
items.text: Once you are in the RSBSA, you can apply for DA help. That help includes loans, crop and livestock insurance, seeds, fertilizer, farm inputs, technical help and soil analysis.

items.title: Buy the rest from licensed dealers
items.text: For what you buy alone, use a dealer licensed by the FPA. Our guide to [fertilizer brands and dealers](/blog/fertilizer-brands-and-dealers) and the page on the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority) explain what to check.

blocks.text: Many cooperatives also work with the DA Agribusiness and Marketing Assistance Service. It helps farmer groups with business planning and market matching. That matters later, when you sell, as our guide to an [online marketplace for farmers](/blog/online-marketplace-for-farmers-philippines) shows.

blocks.title: Check the label, not the post
blocks.text: A group post that says "this spray cured my rice" is a story, not a recommendation. Before you buy, find the active ingredient, then follow the product label and its FPA registration for your crop. If the post names only a brand, ask what the active ingredient is.
Is a premium membership worth paying for?

Pay only for what you will use. A cooperative fee pays for group buying, credit and a share of the profits. A farm app plan pays for tools. Most online farmer groups are free, so a fee to simply join a chat group is hard to justify.

On anee.io there is no separate community membership. You get the community on every plan. Paid plans add tools for running the farm, and they open more of the community. The prices below are in Philippine pesos.

How does the anee.io farmer community work?

The [farmer community](/features/farmer-community) sits inside the same app where you plan your season. That is the difference. When you ask about yellow leaves, your crop, its stage and your photos are one tap away.

items: **News feed**: post a photo of your field and growers reply with what worked for them.
**Discussion rooms**: topics such as palay, gulay or pests, where you ask and answer.
**Messages**: talk one to one with photos and voice notes.
**Cofarmers**: connect with growers you trust and keep up with their posts.
**A ladder of 100 levels**: members who help others climb ten titles, so helpful farmers stand out.

blocks.text: If nobody answers, ask Anee, the smart farm technician inside anee.io. She reads your lot, its stage and the weather before she answers, in Tagalog or English. Anee uses credits, and she comes with Libre + Anee and every paid plan. Meanwhile, the [Contact List](/features/farm-contact-list) keeps the suppliers, traders and buyers you meet, with notes and tags, across every season.

blocks.text: What should you post to get good answers?
A vague post gets vague replies. So give people what an agriculturist would ask you first.

items: A close photo of the problem and one photo of the whole field.
The crop and variety, and its age in days after transplanting or sowing.
What you applied and when, with the active ingredient if it was a spray.
The weather of the last week: heavy rain, dry spell or strong wind.
What you want to know: what it is, what to do, or whether to wait.

blocks.text: For a second opinion from a trained person, see where to [ask an agriculturist online](/blog/ask-an-agriculturist-online). The Agricultural Training Institute also runs a Farmers' Contact Center that answers by call, text, email and online chat.
Questions about joining a Filipino farmer community

items.q: Is there a free Filipino farmer community online?
items.a: Yes. Most farmer groups on social media are free, and the anee.io community is free on the Libre plan. Libre also includes a farm diary for one active season. It shows a few ads.

items.q: Can I buy fertilizer and seeds through a farmer community?
items.a: Not through anee.io, which does not sell inputs. Group buying usually happens through a registered cooperative or farmers' association. RSBSA registration also makes you eligible for DA programs that give seeds and fertilizer.

items.q: How do I register in the RSBSA?
items.a: Ask your city or municipal agriculture office for the enrollment form. Bring a valid government ID and, if you farm your own lot, proof of ownership, tenancy or lease. Registration is free and lasts for life.

items.q: Do I need to pay to post in the anee.io community?
items.a: No. Every plan, including Libre, can use the community. Paid plans add full community access and farm tools, and Farm Owner can also create discussion rooms.

items.q: How do I know if advice from a group is safe?
items.a: Ask for the reason behind the advice and the active ingredient behind any product. Then follow the label and its FPA registration for your crop. When in doubt, ask your municipal agriculturist.
